newsitem.title: UK: Blood donation helps AIDS victims and donors-study.
newsitem.headline: Blood donation helps AIDS victims and donors-study.

text.p: A controversial AIDS therapy involving plasma transfusions not only benefits the recipients but helps prevent AIDS in the donors too, British researchers said on Tuesday.

People infected with the HIV virus who donated plasma progressed more slowly to deadly full-blown AIDS, or Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome, Abraham Karpas of Cambridge University and colleagues said.

"We did not envisage this in our wildest dreams," Karpas, a blood specialist, said in a telephone interview. "It appears that donating plasma at regular intervals helps patients actually delay progression to AIDS."

For several years, Karpas and colleagues have been testing a method called Passive Immune Therapy (PIT), which involves taking blood plasma from HIV-positive but healthy donors and giving it to people with AIDS.
Karpas and his collaborators say it works -- that AIDS patients often get better.
"You are passing immunity from people who have it to people who don't have it," he said.
Of 40 AIDS patients being treated in London's Ealing Hospital, about half have shown "significant" benefit, including weight gain, Karpas said.
Other researchers have been sceptical, including Britain's Medical Research Council, which has refused to fund Karpas's work.
His latest findings are published in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, Britain's national academy of sciences.
He said he was faced with a shortage of HIV-positive donors for his PIT tests.
"The bottleneck for passive immunotherapy is getting enough plasma. People used to ask, 'How do you know you are not harming the donors?'," he said.
So they started testing the blood of the donors. "We hoped at best to be able to show that it didn't do them any harm," Karpas said.
"To our great surprise it appears that, not only doesn't it do them any harm, but some of them had an improving T-cell count."
T-cells are the immune system calls that the HIV virus infects. The lower the count, or number of T-cells, the more serious the infection and damage to the immune system.
Karpas said there could be several reasons for his researchers' finding.
Plasma donation involves taking a donor's blood and filtering out all the white blood cells -- the immune system cells -- and red blood cells and putting those back into the donor.
The fluid that is left is the plasma and is given to the donor. It can contain smaller particles such as antibodies, which fight infection along with white blood cells.

Karpas said perhaps temporarily taking away the white blood cells, which include T-cells, may stimulate those remaining to reproduce. Or perhaps those that are taken away are somehow stimulated to reproduce.

Karpas said he felt his findings were significant enough to justify a proper scientific trial, which would involve giving some patients placebo -- not real plasma from HIV-positive donors -- and in which no one knew which patients were getting which treatment.
He said he hoped his findings would encourage more people to get HIV tests.
"Many people who may be in the high-risk group are reluctant to come forward for testing because they know even the best drug combination has a limited effect.
"But now we can tell them it's worthwhile to be tested now. If you become a donor, this by itself is likely to delay progression."
Karpas has an agreement with Medicorp Inc. of Montreal for the technology.
